title: Tears, Lies, and the One Thing Worth Boasting In
summary: Jeremiah longs for endless tears for his people and then wishes he could escape them, because the land is full of lies, slander, and betrayal between neighbors. God will refine and punish them, turn Jerusalem into rubble, and scatter them, because they abandoned his law for the Baals. Professional mourners are summoned to teach a dirge, since death has climbed in through the windows. Then God says that no one should boast in wisdom, strength, or wealth, but only in knowing him, and he warns that outward circumcision without a changed heart counts for nothing.
story: This chapter continues the lament that closed chapter 8 and completes the picture of a society coming apart before the enemy even arrives. Chapters 7 and 8 exposed false trust in the temple and in the Law; chapter 9 exposes the breakdown of ordinary trust between people, and then, in verses 23 and 24, gives one of the clearest statements in the Old Testament of what God actually values. Chapter 10 will contrast the living God with the idols of the nations, closing this second section of the book (chapters 7 to 10).
historical:
The chapter comes from the same general period as chapters 7 and 8, the reign of Jehoiakim (609 to 598 BC), when Judah was caught between Egypt and Babylon and its leaders were divided over which to trust. The social decay described in verses 2 to 8 fits a time of political anxiety, when informers, factions, and self-interest could make every relationship dangerous; Jeremiah himself would soon find his own family and townspeople plotting against him (11:21; 12:6).

Verses 25 and 26 name Judah's neighbors: Egypt to the southwest, Edom, Ammon, and Moab to the east and southeast of the Dead Sea, and desert tribes. Several of these peoples practiced circumcision in some form. Ancient Egyptian evidence shows it was practiced there, and it seems to have been known among other peoples of the region as well. The desert peoples who clip the hair of their temples were Arab tribes whose haircut was distinctive; Israel's law forbade that style (Leviticus 19:27), perhaps because of its association with pagan rites.
cultural:
Professional mourning women were a fixture of ancient funerals across the Near East and are still found in some Middle Eastern cultures. They were skilled in chanting laments, often with set forms and refrains, and a family in grief would hire them to lead the wailing. God tells Judah to send for the most skillful and to teach their daughters to wail, which meant that there would be so much death that the skill would be needed in every household. Verse 21's image of death climbing in through the windows may echo ancient Near Eastern ideas of death or a death-demon entering homes, but it works on its own as a picture of a threat that no locked door can keep out.

The traveler's lodge in the wilderness (verse 2) was a simple shelter for caravans on desert roads, the loneliest place a person could stay. Jeremiah would rather be there than among his own people. Wormwood (verse 15) was a bitter plant, a byword for bitterness and grief, and poisoned water meant that even the most basic necessity had become deadly.
literary: The chapter is mostly poetry. It opens with the prophet's voice (verses 1 and 2) and then passes to God's (verses 3 to 9), ending with the same refrain heard twice in chapter 5: Should I not punish them for these things? Verse 12 asks a question in the style of wisdom literature (Who is the man wise enough to understand this?), and verses 13 to 16 answer it in prose. Verses 17 to 22 are a dirge in the qinah rhythm, the limping meter of Hebrew laments. Verses 23 and 24 are a short, balanced wisdom saying: three false boasts (wisdom, strength, riches) set against the one true one. Verse 4 contains a pun: every brother deals craftily translates aqov yaaqov, which also means every brother is a Jacob, recalling the patriarch who deceived his brother Esau.

outline.t: The prophet's tears and his wish to escape
Tongues like bows: a nation of liars
Summon the wailing women: death at the windows
Boast only in knowing the LORD

doctrines.note: Verse 24 is one of the Old Testament's great summaries of God's character: he exercises loving devotion (chesed), justice, and righteousness on the earth, and he delights in them. To know God is to know a God of this kind.

The chapter shows sin corroding trust at the level of friendship and family: lies, slander, betrayal, speaking peace while planning harm. Refusing to know God and refusing to tell the truth are presented as one condition.
True wisdom is not cleverness, strength, or wealth but understanding and knowing the LORD. Human achievement becomes a false boast when it is trusted in place of him.

words.note: Aqav, to supplant, overreach, or deal craftily, the root behind the name Jacob (Yaaqov), which Genesis 25:26 and 27:36 link with grasping and deceiving. In verse 4 every brother deals craftily, literally every brother Jacobs his brother. The people have become like their ancestor at his worst, and the old story of family deception has become a whole society's way of life.

Halal, in this form to boast or glory. It is the same root as hallelujah, praise the LORD. Verses 23 and 24 use it five times: people will glory in something, and the only question is what. Boasting in God is the right form of the same impulse that goes wrong in boasting in ourselves.

Chesed, loving devotion or steadfast love, the loyal, covenant-keeping love that God shows to his people. It heads the list of what God does and delights in (verse 24). Set beside justice and righteousness, it shows that God's love and his justice are not rivals but belong together.

Orlah, foreskin. Verse 26 says the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart. Circumcision was the sign of the covenant, but the sign was meant to express a heart devoted to God. Without that, the circumcised are no different from the nations around them.

christ: Paul quotes the heart of verses 23 and 24 twice: let the one who boasts boast in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31; 2 Corinthians 10:17). In 1 Corinthians 1 he applies it to the cross, where God has overturned the world's wisdom, strength, and status, and he identifies Christ as the wisdom and power of God. For Paul, to know the LORD who exercises steadfast love, justice, and righteousness is to know him in Christ crucified. The warning about those circumcised yet uncircumcised is taken up in Romans 2:25-29, where Paul says true circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, and Colossians 2:11 speaks of a circumcision not done by hands in Christ. The prophet's tears for the slain daughter of his people also anticipate Jesus's tears over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41).

hard.q: Verse 16 says God will pursue his people with the sword until he has finished them off, but elsewhere he says he will not make a full end. Which is it?
hard.a:
Jeremiah contains both kinds of statement. Verse 16 speaks of a sword sent after the scattered people until they are consumed, and 9:11 of Jerusalem made a heap of rubble. Yet 4:27 and 5:10, 18 say that God will not make a full end, and later chapters promise return and restoration (chapters 29 to 33). Interpreters reconcile these in a few ways. Many see a distinction between the nation as a political and religious order, which was indeed brought to an end in 586 BC, and the people as a whole, a remnant of whom would survive and return. Others note that prophetic poetry speaks in the strongest terms to break through complacency, while the book as a whole shows that judgment is never God's last word.

Critical scholars often add that the book gathers oracles from different moments and editors, some spoken before the fall in unqualified terms and some shaped afterward in light of the exile and the hope of return. On any of these readings, the tension is real and deliberate: the judgment is total enough to end the old order, and God's mercy is deep enough that the end is not final.

questions: Jeremiah wished he could leave his people and also wept for them. Have you ever felt both at once toward a person or community? What did you do with it?
What are you most tempted to boast in: your wisdom, strength, or wealth? What would it look like to boast instead in knowing God?
Verse 24 says God delights in loving devotion, justice, and righteousness. How should that shape what you delight in?
